Transition metal (TM) catalyzed cross-coupling reactions are the utmost versatile and reliable methods for the production of many industrially important fine chemicals. The utilization of transition metals nanocatalysts in organic transformations, specifically the Suzuki, Heck, and Sonogashira cross-coupling reactions, have enticed the vigilant eye of researchers and technologists due to; (i) high surface area, (ii) higher number of surface atoms leading to large number of catalytic active centers, and (iii) chemical stability. Moreover, being colloidal, nanomaterials combine the properties of both homogeneous and heterogeneous. i.e., solubility in different solvents and ease in the separation of catalysts. This improves the overall catalytic efficiency and cost. Therefore, these pseudo-homogeneous nanocatalysts are gaining a great deal of attention due to their broad substrate scope and ease of handling. This review article focuses on the recent advances in developing nanostructured catalysts and their utilization for selective carbon–carbon bond-forming reactions, e.g., Suzuki, Heck, and Sonogashira coupling reactions. The main focus is laid on the reactions catalyzed by nanocatalysts derived from transition metals such as Pd, Pt, Cu, Ag, Ni, Fe, Au, and Zn, expounding the conception and rationale based on the reactivity improvement and the recyclability of the nanocatalysts are presented here. The heterogeneous catalysis, essential in daily chemical transformations, is demonstrated, implicating significant functions presented by the nanocatalysts, related pros and cons, recyclability, and efficiency.

1. Introduction

TM-catalyzed cross-coupling reactions are amongst the most powerful tools that find widespread applications in synthesizing natural products, functional materials, pharmaceuticals, and agrochemicals [1,2]. Among them, Suzuki-Miyaura (Suzuki), Mizoroki-Heck (Heck), and Sonogashira cross-coupling reactions are considered the most versatile and broadly applied reactions for the formation of C<sub>A</sub>C, C@C, and C„C, respectively [3,4] (Scheme 1).

These three reactions have significant practical and theoretical significance in pharmaceuticals, polymers, and natural product synthesis. These reactions are also used for the intra-cellular synthesis of therapeutic molecules [5]. Traditionally, these reactions are catalyzed by homogeneous Pd-complexed catalysts and ligands such as phosphor and N-heterocyclic carbene [6–8]. Despite signif icant advancements in attaining higher activity, enhanced selectivity, and broader substrate scope, homogeneous Pd catalysts suffer from liabilities such as toxicity and post-processing procurement of most of the ligands used, expensive downstream separation [9] of residual metal from the final product below the maximum allowable level, and reusability of the catalyst [10]. Moreover, the use of toxic solvents, cumbersome multi-step synthesis involved in their preparation, tedious handling due to their air sensitivity, and laborious chromatographic purification of the product also pose a challenge. Consequently, homogeneous Pd catalysts are far from industrial realism [11,12].

Recently, heterogeneous metal catalysis has been gaining much attention due to its superior catalytic activity, broad substrate scope, and ease of handling [13]. The nanocatalysts are easy to recover by filtration or centrifugation, allowing reusability of the catalyst after the completion of the reactions [3,14,15]. A great part of the former heterogenous catalysis community is emerging into the nanoparticle community, as highlighted in the special issue of the prestigious journal ‘‘Chem. Rev.”(nanocatalysts) [16]. Moreover, nanocatalysts-based transformation is considered a nonhazardous and greener approach, which is desirable for sustainability and economic viability [17]. In addition, nanocatalysts that are built up on TM nanoparticles (NPs) such as Au, Cu, Pd, and their alloys can drive a wide range of C C cross-coupling reactions and C-Het (N, S, N) bond formations with enhanced catalytic activity, broad substrate scope, and improved yields [15]. These catalyst systems are generally free from ligands and the requirement of air and moisture-sensitive conditions [15]. Materials in the nanosize regime bear the highest surface area and the highest number of surface atoms that can be further tuned through the synthesis method employed. This leads to higher catalytic efficiency due to; (i) increasing the contact between the substrate and catalytic center, (ii) offering many catalytic active sites per unit volume as compared to bulk heterogeneous counterpart, (iii) higher zeta potential values, and (iv) due to unique surface chemistry associated with the nanomaterials [18,19].

Consequently, TM NPs based nanocatalysts have emerged as promising alternatives to conventional homogeneous complexes and demonstrated a plethora of applications in medicinal chemistry, electronics, and industrial settings [20–23]. In particular, the application of TM NPs based nanocatalysts in Suzuki, Heck, and Sonogashira cross-coupling reactions has witnessed phenomenal growth in the past decade. For instance, a search on Scopus for articles published since 2010 on the subject matter described in this review is illustrated in Fig. 1.

The data show that in recent years, there has been remarkable growth in the utility of nanocatalysts for coupling reactions. However, issues of their low selectivity, the requirement of harsher reaction conditions, leaching of metal species from the support, and side product formation need to be addressed [24]. Likewise, the controversy of whether it is the surface of NPs (heterogeneous pathway) or the leached metal species in the solution (homogeneous pathway) involved in the catalysis process also requires further attention. As a result, searching for efficient pseudo-homogeneous nanocatalysts with superior performance to relinquish the liabilities of the homogenous transition metals catalysts remains an ongoing challenge within the field [23,25]. In this contribution, the development progress for synthesizing colloidal nanocatalysts has paved the way to address some of these questions [26–29].

Likewise, the architectures of well-defined nanostructured supporting materials have also made meaningful advancements in the field [30–32]. The use of nanocatalysts of TM NPs is considered a process involving TM NPs on the nanoscale (1 nm to 100 nm in diameter) on solid support $( \mathrm { e . g . } , \mathrm { S i O } _ { 2 } , \mathrm { A l } _ { 2 } \mathrm { O } _ { 3 } , \mathrm { F e } _ { 2 } \mathrm { O } _ { 3 } ,$ $\mathsf { M g O } , \mathsf { C e O } _ { 2 } , \mathsf { T i O } _ { 2 } ,$ , and others) as solid catalysts and reactants of dif ferent phases (e.g., gas or liquid). Generally, the NPs are grown onto a support surface such as alumina, silica, or carbon-based material by impregnation of metal salts, followed by the reduction of these precursors salts to zero-valent metal NPs [33]. These systems are, therefore, up-and-coming for their potential utilization in the industry [34].

Since these supports and resulting nanocatalysts bear a high surface area, even small amounts of dispersed metal NPs onto support can lead to higher efficiency when compared with their bulk counterpart (larger size particles) [35–37]. Moreover, the dexterity to integrate the precise nano-sized (1 to 100 nm (Fig. 2) [38,39] objects into the nanostructured composite affords unprecedented opportunities to generate multiple catalytic interfaces with the elaborated spatial arrangement on a single platform to exploit their synergistic effects [40].

Earlier review articles that summarize applications of nanocatalysts in cross-coupling reactions are relatively specific, such as A<sup>3</sup> (aldehyde, amine, alkyne) coupling reactions [42,43], Pd NPS catalyzed polyols coupling reactions [44], while some are majorly concentrated on either composition of the nanocatalyst used or the type of reaction explored. For example, Somorjai et al. reviewed the main concepts of using metal nanoparticles in organic transformation [39]. Some other group-published work includes diverse organic transformations by selective metals (mostly Pd, Pt) nanocatalysts [40–43] with a focus on C C and/ C–X coupling reactions catalyzed [44,45]. Astruc and co-workers explored the metal NPs catalyzed semi-heterogeneous catalysis as a frontier among heterogeneous and homogeneous catalysis [47]. Likewise, another short review on TM NPs catalyzed C C bond construction highlights the nanocatalysts role in an aqueous medium for catalytic C C bond formation [48]. Recently, a detailed review of the polyol synthesis of Pd NPs with different sizes and shapes and their use in cross-coupling and hydrogenation reactions were reported [44]. Recently, Hong et al. reviewed the use of Pd nanoparticles with a special focus on the role of support materials on the in Pd-NPs catalyzed Suzuki, Heck, and Sonogashira crosscoupling reactions [49]. To the best of our knowledge, a comprehensive review dedicated to different TM NPs (Pd, Pt, Cu, Ni, Fe, Au, Ag, and Zn) nanocatalysts is lacking in the literature. Therefore, in this review, we will summarize recent advances in Suzuki, Heck, and Sonogashira cross-coupling reactions catalyzed by TM nanocatalysts, focusing on literature reports majorly spanning from the year 2010 to 2021. We begin with the design of nanocatalysts, with a focus on the size, shape, and role of support material. Then we will give recent advances in transition metals (Pd, Pt, Cu, Ni, Fe, Au, Ag, and Zn) NPs catalyzed C C bond-forming reactions. Lastly, we will conclude and give the future prospects and main challenges of the field.

2. The design of nanocatalysts

The nanocatalysts catalytic efficiency, selectivity, and recyclability depend on the nanoparticles’ size, shape, composition, and assembly, and their instauration with the support. Nanocatalysts may be deigned as nanocrystals, clusters of metals, metals oxide, and nonoxides of various sizes and shapes. These may involve no support materials or may be supported on carbonaceous materials, polymers, metal oxide, or porous materials such as siliceous mesocellular foam [50]. The rational design of nanocatalysts is important to achieve enhanced catalytic activity, chemical and thermal stability, selectivity, and high efficiency [51]. The tailored nanomaterials would necessitate tuning their chemical and physi cal properties as efficient nanocatalysts through particle size, shape, surface composition, and surface reactivity [52]. It is widely known that electron transfer occurs between the catalyst surface and the reactive species in all key steps of the catalytic reactions, including the reactants adsorption, intermediates diffusion, and the desorption of the products [53]. Thus, tuning the spatial and energy distribution of valence electrons at the catalyst surface would enhance the catalytic efficiency, such as the activation energy barrier, which in turn is linked to the reactivity and selectivity of the catalysts [54,55]. Based on frontier molecular orbital theory, adsorption and bonding of reactants on the surface of the catalyst are dependent upon matching their energy levels to those of the catalyst surfaces as well as the symmetry and spin state of the reactant’s molecular or atomic orbitals [56,57]. These properties of nanomaterials can be achieved/tuned by altering their size, lattice framework, morphology, quantum size, and electronic effects from nanopore confinement [58–65]. Likewise, the support’s size, shape, and composition are critically important in the design of catalysts [62,63]. In addition, nanocatalysts’ thermal and chemical stability is also very important since catalysts can be deactivated because of surface aggregation, leaching, phase changes, and sintering [64,65].
2.1. Size effect

One of the foremost importance of using nanocatalysts is their small size because this is directly linked with other parameters such as high surface area, chemical stability, and reactivity responsible for the enhanced catalytic activities. Therefore, in the past year, enormous work has been dedicated to nanosized catalysts to understand the effect of particle size on their catalytic and electronic properties in numerous transformations, more specifically, coupling reactions [66,67]. When the size of the NPs decreases, the ratio of surface to the bulk atoms increases, denoting that more surface atoms eventually be accessible for the reactions. However, catalytic activity is not often in direct proportion with the increased surface area of smaller NPs [68]. The surface of nanocatalysts with assorted facets can offer diverse binding force strength and configuration, which prolong different active sites, steps, and corners of surface terraces. Therefore, the size and shape of the NPs significantly affect their catalytic performance [69–76]. Likewise, exposure of the crystallographic planes and accessibility of catalyst active sites fitted into the porous structure onto the solid support is also critical for catalytic activity and selectivity [73,74]. The higher performance of nanocatalysts is considered due to the phenomenon of nano-effects, which is believed to result due to structural, quantum size, and electronic effects [58,59,75].

The wet impregnation method is a widely employed technique for preparing transition metal nanocatalysts [76]. However, compared to the solution-phase synthesis of metal nanoparticles, the impregnation method offers poor control over the particle size and size distribution of resulting metal NPs. Nevertheless, the method is still prevalent today due to its scope of scalability and low cost. Other methods for the synthesis of metal nanocatalysts include coprecipitation, which could be in-situ precipitation of the metal and the support using sol–gel protocols [77] or using post-functionalization to deposit the colloidal nanoparticles onto the support [78] or polymer-assisted method that involves polymer as a template to nucleate and stabilize NPs [79,80]. A decrease in the size of the catalyst produces a dominant effect on the surface atoms at edges and corner positions [81,82]. This affects the catalytic activity by creating under-coordinating states on the surfaces. It was found that the fractions of metals on surface atoms having coordination numbers of 4,7,9 in octahedral NPs or 3,6,8 cubic NPs present strong dependences on the size of NPs [83]. The correlation results shown in Fig. 3 illustrate the dependence of catalytic performance on the size NPs.

The general tendency of increased catalytic activity with the particle size decreases indicates that the low coordination number of vertex and edge atoms on the particle surface are active sites for the Suzuki reaction [85] Fig. 4. Further, a series of well-defined homopolymer-stabilized Pd colloids with varying metal particle sizes was utilized to investigate the Heck coupling reaction of olefine and aryl halides [86]. A low reaction rate was obtained when the Pd precursor was utilized without a polymer, implying the reaction doesn’t occur through solution-phase catalysis by leached Pd particles. A quantitative relationship was found between the initial reaction rates over various stabilized Pd NPS and the number of low-coordinated (defect) Pd surface atoms calculated using statistics for face-centered cubic (fcc) cuboctahedron [87]. Initial reaction rates did not vary, calculated per number of the defect atoms. The Pd- NPs catalyzed Heck coupling of aryl halides with olefins was thus so-called to be a structure-sensitive reaction with low-coordinated atoms as active sites (Fig. 5). These findings agree with the results for the supported Pd catalyst in the Suzuki coupling reaction [66].

According to the d-band center theory, the catalyst’s reactivity depends on the d-band valence electrons near the Fermi level. Consequently, the reactant adsorption, activation, and dissociation are directly related to that metal’s d-band center of gravity [95]. Therefore, tuning the spatial and energy distribution of the valence electrons at the surface is important for the reactivity and selectivity of the catalyst. The current literature widely suggests that adsorption energies dependent upon the size of adsorbates on the surface of catalyst atoms rely on the coordination numbers [96–103]. For instance, the surface atoms of catalysts with low orbitals coordina tion numbers exhibit more adsorption for a specific molecule than higher coordination numbers [84,100]. Computational studies have also suggested that the activation energies of adsorbate for the chemisorption on the surface of Pt NPs catalyst decreases with size. This means activation energies also depend on the size of NPs due to size-dependent cohesive energy, which in turn dictates the size-dependent fraction present on the coordinated surface atoms in nanocatalysts [101]

To conclude, size is one of the key parameters influencing any catalyst’s catalytic performance, especially transition metalsbased nanocatalysts in different chemical reactions [102]. Its influence is complicated in many cases, such as if the rate-determining step is the dissociation of an intra-molecular bond of a reactant molecule, then it is expected that the metal atom has a lower coordination number and exhibits higher catalytic activity [103–109]. Metal atoms with smaller coordination numbers on the surface have stronger adsorption energy, which could reduce the activation barrier to dissociate the reactant molecules and hence accelerate the catalytic process. The size-dependent catalytic activity is favored when the dissociation step acts as the rate-determining step. While in some cases, this trend is opposite to the above statement, in that case, the metal surface atoms have lower coordination numbers, dramatically dissociate a chemical bond, and tightly bind the dissociated species. Still, unfortunately, this tightly binding could poison the surface of the catalyst to slow down the rate of the chemical reaction when coupling with another species during the catalytic reaction cycle [84,103,106,107].

text: 2.2. Shape effect

The shape of NPs plays a significant role in the catalytic performance of nanocatalysts since NPs with different shapes are synthesized by stabilizing certain facets and allowing the other facets to grow [108,109]. This strategy could tune the synthesis with nanocatalysts with exposed active facets and defined atoms on the corners and edges [110,111]. Packing the atoms in nanocatalyst surfaces has been found in various shapes such as spherical, cubic, tetrahedron, octahedron, and truncated octahedron [112–119]. It has been demonstrated that contrasting atomic arrangements and interactions of different crystal faces of the same crystal could have significantly different distributions of valence electrons, resulting in entirely different molecular adsorption and reactivity [116,117]. Thus, the controlled design of the metal NPs crystals with uniform surface facets is necessary for enhanced catalytic activity and selectivity of the product [118]. These surfaces of metal NPs with specific shapes are composed of either pure (100) facets, pure (111), or vicinal surfaces with (730) facets containing denser steps or kinked atoms that result in lowering the coordination number [119]. Therefore, controlled synthesis of these shapes provides the prospects to systematically explore the surface structure to tune the catalytic activity and selectivity of the catalytic reactions in organic synthesis [84,111]. The lowindex facets such as (100), (110), and (111) of magnetic nanoparticles (MNPs) are preferably exposed due to the lower surface energy and hence more stability. The variations in structural aspects stem mainly from the differences in the atomic packing on the catalyst surfaces [120]. Therefore, the structural variations between different crystallographic surfaces intrinsically influence the dissociation, adsorption, coupling, and interactions of the adsorbed intermediates in the catalytic reactions [84].

A good fraction of the catalysis research was devoted to tailoring metal deposits’ shape on oxide surfaces. One parameter that controls the particle geometry is the metal-support interaction, which is typically small for wide-gap oxides, causing the metals to grow in a 3D fashion [121]. Various approaches were developed to modify this parameter, for instance, by introducing defects and species (OH functionalities) into the oxide surface or using polar oxide terminations with high metal oxide adhesion[122]. Alternatively, electron-transfer processes across the metal oxide interface may be exploited to alter the growth morphology of metals. This approach has been demonstrated for thin fil oxides on metal support first [123]. The shapes of metal nanoparticles, particularly in wet chemistry synthesis, can be controlled in the twilight zone of kinetic and thermodynamic control [115]. This is mostly controlled by the capping ligands, solvents, and temperature by controlling the nucleation and growth steps [124–130]. El-Sayed et al. reported that Pt NPs have cubic, tetrahedral, and spherical spiracles shapes (Fig. 6). These shapes were controlled by altering the concentration of capping materials to the concentration of Pt cations used in the reductive hydrogen method at room temperature [127]. Later on, the same research group reported the Pt NPs with various shapes as nanocatalysts for electron transfer reactions [66,128]. The tetrahedral-shaped Pt NPs showed excellent catalytic activity with the lowest activation energy (14 kJ mol<sup>1</sup>), whereas cubic-shaped Pt NPs exhibited low catalytic activity, having the highest activation energy (26.4 kJ mol<sup>1</sup>). The sphericle-shaped Pt NPs displayed moderate catalytic activity due to exposed facets and fewer catalytically active atoms on the surface of NPs. Thus, tetrahedral-shaped Pt NPs exhibiting (111) facets had a large fraction of atoms on the edges and corners of the surface. On the other hand, cubic-shaped Pt NPs contained (100) facets on the surface with smaller fractions of atoms on the edges and corners of the surfaces. Due to these exposed facets and catalytically active atoms on the surface of tetrahedral NPs, the tetrahedral Pt NPs proved more active than cubic Pt NPs [128].

The shape dependence of NPs on the reactivity in C C bond formation, e.g., in the Suzuki reaction, has been demonstrated by Bokhoven et al. [74]. The catalytic activity tends to increase from spherical to tetrahedral shapes of Pt NPs, which was linked to the (111) facets of tetrahedral shapes that bear the maximum catalytically active sites on the surface of NPs. Likewise, Huang reported the synthesis of Pd nanorods and branched Pd nanostructures for the C C coupling reaction [129,130]. The study concluded that both nanorods and branched NPs were proved to be very active catalysts with comparable chemical stability and recyclabil ity. However, the nanorods had a little edge (92 % yield) over star shape (90 % yield).

text: 2.3. Support materials

In the case of supported metal catalysis, the support materials have been considered to be inert, and their prime role was to increase the stability of the metal particles by immobilizing and dispersing them to improve the active surface area. Later, the Tauster group introduced the term strong metal-support interaction to elaborate on the unexpected chemisorption properties of $\mathrm { H } _ { 2 }$ on noble metal NPs supported by $\mathrm { T i O } _ { 2 }$ [63]. Further, the importance of the support materials has been explored at a fundamental level, commonly utilizing model catalysts. In short, the role of the support materials in catalysis is somewhat more complex and yet to be explored. Support material can play direct or indirect roles during a catalytic transformation. These provide precise defect sites onto which the metal NPs can be immobilized in the case of metastable particles [131]. In addition, the support can enable the electronic interactions between metal NPs and provide functionalities to the nanomaterials, such as acidic sites or basic sites that improve the stability, activity, and selectivity of the catalyst [132,133].

Earlier studies have shown that the catalysts inherent activity and selectivity may vary strongly, contingent on the size of the metal NPs (>7 nm in diameter). Yet the size is not solely responsible for varying catalyst efficiencies. The choice of catalyst support is captious even for materials having the same geometry, for which mass transport differences can be ruled out [13]. This frequently turns out that some support materials catalyze unwanted side transformations, in many cases, the clarification is less frivolous [134]. In some cases, the NPs catalytic activity decreased upon recyclability. Therefore, a stabilizer such as a polymer ligand and surfactant was used to overcome the mentioned issues [135]. A series of supporting materials such as CNTs [136], colloidal support [137], silica [137], metal NPs support [138], polymers [139], carbon [140], and graphene [141] have been reported. On the other hand, using magnetic NPs as catalyst support could also enable the effective separation of catalysts from the reaction mixture with the help of an external magnet [142]. In summary, the nanostructured support materials hosting the active metal NPs nanocatalysts significantly reduce the overall cost, provide simple and scalable preparation, and easy filtration for efficient recycling [143].
3. Transition metals NPs catalyzed CC bond-forming reactions
3.1. Pd NPs catalyzed C<sub>A</sub>C bond-forming reactions

Palladium nanoparticles are utilized in various C C coupling reactions [144,145], which are the essential methodologies of modern organic synthesis. A one-step approach can achieve various aryl derivatives with high yield and selectivity without isolating the intermediate products. Pd NPs catalyzed cross-coupling reactions are well documented by different research groups [46,146,147]. The Pd NPs can be immobilized on different supports. In this context, Liew et al. recently reported the immobilization of Pd NPs onto fluorine-doped tin oxide (FTO) support. The nanocatalyst was employed in Suzuki coupling reactions of aryl halides and phenylboronic acid to construct biphenyl in reasonably high yields (up to 80 %). The Pd nanocatalysts showed a high degree of chemical stability [148]. In another study, Mahmoud et al.

The nanocatalysts proved efficient as the reactions required a very low catalyst loading (0.005 mol%). Moreover, the Boehmite surface was proved to be an excellent stabilizer for supporting Pd NPs, since nanocatalysts could be reused after repeated 8 cycles without a considerable loss of catalytic activity (Scheme 2) [149].

To further provide stability to the catalyst, the support materials should have more anchoring sites, such as nitrogen-containing functional groups (e.g., amino groups) or nitrogen-doped carbonbased materials to immobilize metal NPs. This covalent binding of metal NPs increases the stability of the prepared catalyst. In this contribution, Liu et al. encapsulated the Pd NPs in a nanoscale amine-functionalized tubular silica support to form a physically confined nanocatalyst with a high specific surface area. These structural features were favourable for good dispersion of Pd NPs, simple and fast mass transport of reactants, and easy access of reactants to active sites. Finally, the nanocatalyst was utilized for the Suzuki coupling reaction with 98 % yield of the coupling product (Scheme 3) [150].

Nanostructure alumina was treated with different quantities of PdCl (1,5-cyclooctadiene) to promote the formation of supported Pd NPs, which were then reduced in situ in a single step to give dispersed Pd NPs as catalysts [151]. The prepared materials were tested in a specific C C Suzuki coupling reaction (Scheme 4). This is maybe due to two different effects, first the possible agglomeration of the NPs after the first cycle, which has been previously reported [152]. In contrast, the second reason may be an additional effect related to the carboxy functional group. Recently, our group has reported Pd NPs functionalized onto highly reduced graphene oxide (HRG) as nanocatalyst for the Suzuki coupling reactions in water (Scheme 5) [153]. The nanocatalysts system did not require any pre-activation or inert reaction conditions. 1-aminopyrene stabilized the Pd NPs on the surface of graphene. The density of the Pd NPs was increased through aminopyrene functionalization, where the amine group provides the nucleation site for Pd NPs. Likewise, the amino groups also helped to avoid aggregation and agglomeration of the NPs. The nanocatalyst was used for the coupling reaction of various aryl halides with pyreneboronic acid to yield 1-phenylpyrene in excellent conversion (up to 100 %).

The turnover frequency (TOF) values for HRG-Pd and HRG-Py Pd were calculated and compared, which were 197 h<sup>1</sup> and 1000 h<sup>1</sup>, respectively. To investigate the substituent effect, the per formance of as-prepared nanocatalyst HRG-Py-Pd was evaluated for the Suzuki coupling reaction of bromo, chloro, and iodo benzene and other several types of substituted aryl halides having both the electron donating groups (EDG) and electronwithdrawing groups (EWG) with variation of phenyl boronic acid in aqueous conditions. Besides these, the catalytic efficiency of HRG-Py-Pd nanocatalyst was tested for other various substituted aryl halides such as 40- bromoacetophenone, 4-chlorobenzenephenone and 4- bromoanisol. The substituted aryl halides have slightly shown a lesser amount of conversion efficiency than the non-substituted aryl halides due to steric hindrance present in these substituents. For example, 4- bromoanisole containing EDG (methoxy group) demonstrated 100 % conversion efficiency compared with 4- chlorobenzophenone consisting of (78.9 % conversion) as shown below in Fig. 7 [153].

These parameters also tune the morphologies of the resulting Pd nanostructure, e.g., spherical, dendritic, rectangular, and triangular-shaped Pd [170]. Depending upon morphology, these nanostructured nanocatalysts can alter the activity and selectivity of the reaction product. For example, Kamal et al. synthesized the Pd NPs supported onto carbon spheres. The nanocatalyst was utilized for the Heck coupling reaction, resulting in significantly high activity (98 % yield of the product) (Scheme 11) [171]. The dispersion of the Pd NPs on the carbon surface leads to high activity and selectivity [172].

In quest of simplifying nanocatalyst recovery and reusability, Arash et al. prepared the heterogeneous Pd nanoparticles bound to $\mathrm { F e } _ { 3 } { \cal O } _ { 4 } \mathrm { N P s }$ through -S-methylisothiourea ligand (Pd-SMU-$\mathsf { M N P s } ) \left[ 1 7 7 \right] .$ . The nanocatalyst was then employed for the Suzuki cross-coupling reaction between diverse aryl halides and phenylboronic acid to produce a variety of biaryls in reasonably good yields (up to 97 %). Using magnetic NPs (MNPs) as support was attractive since the nanocatalysts could be rapidly recovered from the reaction contents using an external magnet. The nanocatalyst exhibited considerable catalytic activity (95 % yield of the product) without a significant loss for consecutive 8 runs (Scheme 12) [173].

Naghipour et al. also adopted a similar strategy by coating magnetic nanoparticles (MNPs) core with a shell of chitosan, which was then tailored with Schiff base ligand followed by immobilization of Pd NPs to produce heterogeneous nanocatalyst $( \mathrm { F e _ { 3 } O _ { 4 } @ C S - S c h i f f }$ base Pd). As a green solvent, an enhanced catalytic activity and product conversion for the Suzuki coupling reaction was achieved in polyethylene glycol (PEG). In the case of the Heck coupling reaction, DMF was found to be the better solvent for a higher product yield of 98 %. The catalytic activity of the recovered catalyst from the reaction was almost unchanged after five cycles.

Further, to avoid the agglomeration of the NPs, the Sekar group synthesized the Pd NPs stabilized with organic corona and employed them as reusable catalysts for C C bond-forming reactions (Scheme 14) [176]. The nanocatalyst exhibited high catalytic activity, providing the corresponding biphenyls and diphenylethene derivatives in good to excellent yields (up to 96 %). Besides, the nanocatalyst could be quantitatively recovered and reused without appreciable catalytic activity loss. Due to the higher Pd-C bond strength, the enhanced catalytic activity was linked to the high stabilization of the Pd NPs with organic shells. This, in turn, helps in restricting the agglomeration of the NPs and maintaining the intact particle size. Antonio Monopoli and his co-workers reported the electrochemical impregnation of Pd NPs over tetragonal zirconium oxide nanopowders. The electrochemically impregnated $\mathrm { P d } / \mathrm { Z r } 0 _ { 2 }$ was demonstrated as an efficient metal-based nanocatalyst for coupling reactions (Suzuki and Heck) of aryl halides in an aqueous environment. While during the coupling reactions, the phase transfer catalyst and base tetrabutylammonium hydroxide (TBAOH) produced an emulsified reaction mixture, which overcame the solubility issues of low polar materials in water conditions [177].

The GO-Pd was utilized as a nanocatalyst for Suzuki and Heck coupling reactions [180]. The catalyst could be easily recovered from the reaction without showing any significant change in the surface morphology as monitored by SEM analysis. Moreover, the recovered catalyst could be reused up to five times without any significant loss of catalytic activity [180]. In the Sonogashira reaction, the cross-coupling of aryl or vinyl halides with terminal alkynes to produce conjugated enynes and aryl alkynes is also catalyzed by Pd, using copper (I) as a cocatalyst. The reaction finds many applications in synthesizing natural products, pharmaceuticals, and other important molecular frameworks [183–190]. Although Pd-catalyzed Sonogashira reaction- under homogenous conditions that employ complexes of Pd(II) salts and phosphine ligands display high activity, it is quite challenging to recover from reaction mixtures [187]. This makes its recycling complicated for reuse [187]. Therefore, the heterogeneous Pd nanocatalysts, consisting of an active catalytic Pd species supported on solid support, have been a focus of recent research interest from the scientific community [114–120].

Polanski et al. developed a novel methodology for a coppersupported Pd nanocatalyst by transferring nanoparticles to the target Cu by intermediate carrier SiO [188]. The as-prepared bimetallic Pd/PdO/Cu nanocatalyst was then used for a series of Sonogashira reactions. The Pd/PdO/Cu was a highly efficient and selective catalyst for the reaction between aryl halides and various terminal acetylenes, giving yields from 63 to 100 % of the corresponding products (Scheme 16) [188]. Ultrasonication was employed to prevent the aggregation of NPs and retain the cat alytic activity. Moreover, the recycling of catalysts was facilitated through catalyst separation from the reaction mixture using centrifugation. In addition, a known amount of phosphine ligand was used in each round of the cycle to stabilize and inhibit catalyst deactivation. The performance of the nanocatalysts was proved to be unchanged within the two repeated cycles (100 % conversions). The role of Cu was regarded as two folds; (i) as solid support and (ii) as co-catalyst. The high catalytic activity of the bimetallic nanocatalysts was linked to the coexistence of PdO species, which was developed in the Pd/Cu system as revealed by X-ray photo electron spectroscopy (XPS) analysis [188].

In 2005 Astruc et al., summarized the research work in the field of Pd-based nanocatalysts for coupling reactions under ambient conditions. He concluded that the low generation of metallodendrimers or metallosters usually optimizes the efficiency and recyclability of catalysts [190]. Later in 2007, they reviewed Pd NPs as catalysts in ${ \mathsf { C } } { - } { \mathsf { C } }$ coupling reaction as homogeneous or heterogeneous pre-catalysts and whether these NPs are intentionally performed or produced from Pd derivatives such as Pd $( { \mathsf { O A c } } ) _ { 2 } .$ Among the coupling reactions, the most studied is the Heck coupling reaction of halogenoarenes with olefins, usually using high temperatures (between 120 and 160 C). In the same year, Astruc and coworker investigated the role of loading a low amount of metal nanocatalyst for developing Pd-catalyzed C<sub>A</sub>C coupling reactions such as Suzuki and Heck reactions. They reported that dendrimer stabilized PdNPs (1 ppm) catalyze Suzuki reaction under ambient conditions [192]. Besides, the lower amount of catalyst loading is crucial for the development of green Pd-assisted nanocatalysts to catalyze C C cross-coupling reactions.[7] Seminal studies from the groups of Beletskaya, Reetz, and de Varies showed the Pd NPs can catalyze Heck and Suzuki-Miyaura reactions with aryl iodide and, in some cases, aryl bromides at parts per million levels [7,193,194]. As a result, researchers coined the term ‘‘homeopathic” Pd catalysis. PdNP size and stabilization type. The TON increased with decreas ing the Pd/substrate ratio, which suggested a leaching mechanism. [195] According to the atom leaching mechanism dendrimer stabilized PdNPs synthesized by using click chemistry approach catalyzed C C cross-coupling reactions under ambient conditions with the homeopathic amount (little as 1 ppm) of PdNPs. It is also investigated that the extraction of these PdNPs from reaction mix ture, which is a complicated task in synthetic chemistry, is possible with the thiols group as catalytically active PdNPs of complemen tary mechanistic interest. Therefore, it is also feasible to determine the influence of NP size on the catalytic parameters (efficiency and stability) and mechanism [192,196]. Recently, the Ali group reported that heterogeneous Pd-based nano catalytic systems $( \mathrm { F e _ { 3 } O _ { 4 } } / \mathrm { P _ { 4 } V P - P d } )$ are recommended as an efficient catalyst for ${ \mathsf { C } } { - } { \mathsf { C } }$ coupling reactions. Due to its high reaction yield (98 %), convenient synthetic process, good biocompatibility of the catalyst, reusability, and economic viability, the $\mathrm { F e _ { 3 } O _ { 4 } / P _ { 4 } V P - P d }$ could be suitable for commercial or industrial applications [197]. Likewise, in another important report, Wei et al. investigated the role of immobilized Pd NPs over pectin-coated magnetic iron oxide $\left( \mathrm { F e } _ { 3 } \mathrm { O } _ { 4 } \right)$ nanomaterials $( \mathrm { F e _ { 3 } O _ { 4 } @ p e c t i n / P d } )$ . The catalyst was easily recovered using a magnet and recycled with insignificant Pd leaching or loss in overall catalytic performance [198]. He and his group synthesized mono and polymetallic Pd complexes having 2-pyridyl-1,2,3- triazole (pyta) and nano branched (nonapyta) ligand using palladium acetate and these ligands by 1:1 ratio and applied as catalysts for C C coupling reactions such as Suzuki, Heck, and Sonogashira coupling reactions. 3.2. Platinum nanocatalyst assisted C<sub>A</sub>C bond-forming reactions

Platinum as nanocatalysts for cross-coupling reaction has been utilized to a limited degree compared to Pd NPs because the oxidative and reductive elimination steps are slower than those of Pd NPs. However, Narayanan et al. have synthesized tetrahedralshaped poly(vinylpyrrolidone) stabilized Pt NPs to catalyze the Suzuki coupling reaction of aryl halide-like iodobenzene and phenylboronic acid (Scheme 17) [66]. They concluded that the morphology of the Pt NPs could be altered from spherical to tetrahedral shape through tailoring reaction parameters which, in return, greatly affect the progress of the Suzuki coupling reaction [200]. In comparison, spherical shape Pt NPs were found to be more active than tetrahedral shapes. However, the authors further investigated that the Pt NPs are not chemically stable under reaction conditions. This leads to a rapid decrease in the catalytic activity of the nanocatalyst.

Specific engineering of nanomaterials shape, size, surface composition, and adsorbed capping ligand is highly important to control selectivity and catalytic activity. This also differentiates the colloidally synthesized Pt-based nano-catalysts from normally used heterogeneous catalysts [201]. Kim et al. developed a block copolymer with tunable micro and mesoporous structure loaded with 2 nm size Pt NPs as a nanocatalyst and utilized in ligand free Suzuki cross-coupling reaction (Scheme 18) [202]. The higher catalytic reactivity and efficiency of Pt-HPP (Hierarchically porous polymer) to a challenging substrate like aryl halide is striking, especially in aryl chloride, where the stronger C-Cl bond disfavor oxidative addition reaction. The screening of the prescribed substrate scope revealed Pt-HPP mostly works well, but electrondeficient substrates lowered the desired yield of selective product. This Pt-loaded polymer support (Pt-HPP) outperformed mesoporous/microporous based supports and indicated higher TOF and better reusability, confirming the hierarchically porous nature of Pt-HPP. It also revealed the superior performance contrasted with analogs of mesoporous silica such as MCF-17 and SBA-15 in terms of TOF, compatibility to green solvents, and especially the substrate’s scope. The hierarchically porous block copolymer has microspores within a 3D continuous mesoporous wall, which was then produced by combining the polymerization-induced micro-phase separation process [203] with hyper cross-linking. The reactant substrate rapidly diffuses through the hierarchically porous structure and accesses the large surface provided by the microspores, where the NPs are anchored. The robust hypercross-linked framework offers high chemical and thermal stability. Further, the catalytic activity of the prepared catalyst was found promising for the Suzuki coupling reaction under mild conditions and ensuring recyclability [204].

Corma synthesized platinum clusters with <5 atoms and used them in base-controlled Suzuki, Heck, and Sonogashira coupling reactions [205]. This computationally explained the basecontrolling effect that rolls out from overcoming the energetic barrier of the oxidative addition and translating the rate-determining of the coupling to alter the step where the base actively contributes [205]. For the Heck C <sub>A</sub> C coupling reactions, Pd and Ni-based catalysts are more frequently reported in the literature. While the other heavier members of its group, such as Pt, barely perform in the same manner. Therefore, there are only some salts or complexes of Pt, catalytically active for Heck reaction due to its dissolution in organic solvents such as dimethylformamide, etc. However, Estefania et al. recently reported Pt NPs as very active species, and these clusters efficiently catalyzed the Heck C C coupling reaction. The author also differentiated the barriers in the first elementary mechanistic steps with small nano-size catalysts (Scheme 19) [205]. These are conventionally found for organometallic compounds and, with the oxidative addition step not the rate-determining step of the reaction. This may be due to the metallic nature of active sites and the participation of bimetallic or trimetallic atoms in the process [13]. It also makes easier cleavage of the $\mathsf C - \mathsf X$ bond of iodo and/or bromobenzene, which allows the higher stabilization of fragments for the required coupling reaction. Consequently, higher activation barriers are required for the coupling step of alkene. Nevertheless, the insertion of only one molecule of each suitable reactant neglects the consequences of co-adsorption of other solvent molecules or reactants was noticed. Certainly, it is precise that the adsorbed solvent molecules may favour the recombination step, which may delay the bond-breaking step in the reactions [205].

3.3. Iron-based nanocatalyst assisted C C bond-forming reactions

Recently, the use of iron (Fe) based catalysts in organic transformations, particularly in C C bond-forming reactions, received significant attention due to their excellent catalytic and magnetic properties [206–215]. In this contribution, iron, as zerovalent or multivalent, is used either as a catalyst or as magnetic support material [209–218]. As an example, Akiyama et al. used sulfurcoated Au-supported iron (0) (SAFe(0)) nanoparticles as ligandfree nanocatalysts for Suzuki coupling and C H amination reaction [212]. Jarvo and co-workers employed the intermolecular cyclization reaction to introduce the quaternary carbon center into the newly formed carbocycles [308], also with the Garg group [309] and the Desrosier group as well [310]. Wang et al. employed a potassium fluoride-alumina-supported nanosized nickel(0) powder catalyst for the Sonogashira reaction [202]. Under microwave irradiation and solvent-free conditions, aromatic and aliphatic terminal alkynes were coupled with aromatic-, heteroaromatic-, and vinyl iodides as coupling partners to produce the corresponding products in good to excellent yield (Scheme 45). The alumina acted as a temperature moderator in the microwave reaction. Liquid reactants with metallic nickel without alumina may lead to uncontrollable reactions.

Zhang’s group has developed a novel method to produce periodic mesoporous silica (PMO) supported Ni(II) organometallic nanocatalyst [311]. The PMO was functionalized with diphenylphosphine ligands and was then utilized as a support to immobilize Ni NPs through coordination interaction. The MPO structure allowed high dispersion of Ni (II) active sites, and the embedded phenyl groups onto the silica walls improved the surface hydrophobicity and promoted the adsorption of reactant molecules onto Ni NPs in an aqueous media. The as-prepared catalyst was employed together with CuI as a co-catalyst in the Sonogashira coupling reaction to produce aryl alkynes in good to excellent yields (Scheme 46). The nanocatalyst exhibited good recyclability, showing no significant activity loss after three repeated cycles.

text: 4. Conclusion and future perspective

This article demonstrates that the TM-based NPs catalyzed C C cross-coupling reactions have witnessed phenomenal growth in the past decade (Fig. 1). The C C coupling transformation finds its utility in producing biomaterials, fine chemicals, natural products, and medicine [315]. More specifically, the Suzuki, Heck, and Sonogashira reactions have been widely exploited to generate diverse structural frameworks and chemical entities. Since homogeneous Pd catalysts are far from industrial realism, heterogeneous metal nanocatalysts have emerged as a promising alternative owing to their superior catalytic activity, broad substrate scope, and ease of handling. Moreover, the ease of recovery and reusability makes their use a non-hazardous and greener approach, which is important for sustainability and economic viability. For a higher catalytic activity, stability, and recyclability of the heterogeneous metal nanocatalysts system, careful design of the nanocatalysts size, shape, and morphology is important. Likewise, the architectures of well-defined nanostructured supporting materials have also made meaningful advancements in the field. Moreover, the dexterity to integrate the precise nano-sized (1 to 100 nm objects into the composite nanostructured affords unprecedented opportunities to generate multiple catalytic interfaces in a single nanostructured catalyst to exploit the synergistic effects between these catalytic interfaces. Mechanistic understanding of a chemical process is equally important. The organic transformations usually follow multistep complex reaction pathways, which need to be fully understood to understand the role of nanocatalysts. A pedagogical approach is required to empower the synthetic chemist with the suitable software and computational chemistry tools needed to design their reaction, prediction flowcharts, and probe reaction pathways was envisioned. Computational chemistry tools such as first principle ab initio and density functional theory could be a strong means to predict the mechanism and kinetics of the chemical transformation. Computational modeling of nanocatalysis due to the variety of nano sizes of the NPs becomes quite complex. Therefore, the theoretical modeling would be an excellent addition to optimize the large number of trials required to explore various configurations corresponding to the different sizes of NPs [316]. Acquiring ‘chemical accuracy’ through computational modeling would necessitate considering all aspects of the catalyst environment, such as support, pressure, temperature, solvent, and other surface-bounds species [317]. The atomistic approaches, combined with machine learning tools, can achieve the desired accuracy required to shape optimum nanocatalysts [318].

Artificial intelligence technology could be a viable solution to solve grand challenges in organic transformations which need in-depth chemical intuition. Advanced hardware, enhanced algorithms, and growing storage capacity would allow scrutinizing variables beyond the ability of human beings and detection of hidden patterns in insignificant and core scale datasheets.
